facts.statement: The genus Pasquiaornis contains two species, P. hardiei and P. tankei, which were described in 1997 by Tim Tokaryk, Stephen Cumbaa, and John Storer.
facts.quote: Two species, P. hardiei and P. tankei, were described in 1997 by Tim Tokaryk, Stephen Cumbaa and John Storer.

facts.statement: Pasquiaornis lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, specifically between 95 and 93 million years ago.
facts.quote: It lived in the Late Cretaceous, during the late Cenomanian between 95 and 93 million years ago in North America.

facts.statement: Later discoveries suggest Pasquiaornis is a basal member of the Hesperornithes, whereas Baptornis represents a more advanced lineage.
facts.quote: Subsequently discovered relatives suggest that it is instead a quite basal member of the Hesperornithes, while Baptornis represents a distinct and somewhat more advanced lineage.

facts.statement: The species P. tankei was approximately one-third larger than P. hardiei and possessed a markedly more robust upper arm.
facts.quote: P.tankei was about one-third larger, with a markedly more robust upper arm

facts.statement: The bones of Pasquiaornis resemble those of the mid-sized Baptornis advenus more closely than the large Hesperornis or Parahesperornis.
facts.quote: The remains look closer to the corresponding bones of the more derived and mid-sized Baptornis advenus than to the large and highly apomorphic Hesperornis and Parahesperornis in shape

facts.statement: Pasquiaornis appears to be one of the most basal lineages within the Hesperornithes.
facts.quote: Pasquiaornis appears to have been one of the most basal lineages.

facts.statement: It is unclear but unlikely that Pasquiaornis, or at least P. tankei, was capable of flight.
facts.quote: whether Pasquiaornis (or at least P.tankei) was still volant is unclear, but unlikely

facts.statement: Pasquiaornis had wings that were poorly adapted for diving compared to other Hesperornithes, and its thickened wing bones were not well suited for flight.
facts.quote: its wing was certainly among the least-adapted to diving among the Hesperornithes, but its wing bones, though resembling those of volant birds, were notably thickened and not well suited for flying either.

facts.statement: Pasquiaornis likely fed on fish and marine invertebrates by diving in the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Like its relatives, these birds probably fed on fish and marine invertebrates, for which they dived in the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: The discovery of at least three P. hardiei and six P. tankei remains in a limited area suggests either mass mortality events or nearby breeding colonies.
facts.quote: The remains referenced in the description encompass at least 3 P.hardiei and 6 P.tankei, found in a fairly limited area, suggesting either mass mortality of a fairly common bird, or nearby breeding colonies that accumulated remains of dead birds over a prolonged time.

facts.statement: The time range for Pasquiaornis is the Cenomanian stage, from 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Cenomanian (100.5 to 93.9 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Fossils of Pasquiaornis were recovered near Arborfield, Saskatchewan, primarily during 1992-1993 expeditions by the Royal Saskatchewan Museum and the Canadian Museum of Nature.
rejected.quote: They are known from fossils recovered near Arborfield, Saskatchewan, mostly by 1992-93 expeditions of the Royal Saskatchewan Museum and the Canadian Museum of Nature.

rejected.statement: Aside from size differences, the two Pasquiaornis species differ in the angle of the femur head and the shape of the foot.
rejected.quote: Apart from size, the Pasquiaornis species differ in the angle of the femur head and the shape of the foot.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'species differ in the angle of the femur'

rejected.statement: Pasquiaornis fossils were found in sedimentary breccia covered by about 4 cm of bentonite, indicating deposition in the shallow waters (less than 6 meters deep) of the Western Interior Seaway following a volcanic eruption.
rejected.quote: The birds' remains were found strewn through patchy sedimentary breccia covered by about 4 cm of bentonite (indicating a major volcanic eruption not too far away), which were probably deposited in the eastern shallows of the Western Interior Seaway in water less than 6 m deep.
